sources.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
sources.text: Our findings reveal that around 80% of the U.S. workforce could have at least 10% of their work tasks affected by the introduction of LLMs, while approximately 19% of workers may see at least 50% of their tasks impacted. Higher-income jobs potentially face greater exposure. The analysis measures exposure of tasks, not whether jobs will be eliminated, and it does not predict the timeline of adoption.

sources.title: Generative AI at Work
sources.text: We study the staggered introduction of a generative AI-based conversational assistant using data from 5,179 customer support agents. Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 14 percent on average, with the greatest impact on novice and low-skilled workers, and minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers.

sources.title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects
sources.text: We examine the labor market effects of AI chatbots using administrative records linked to surveys covering exposed occupations in Denmark, including accountants and financial advisors. Despite substantial investments and widespread adoption, AI chatbots have had no significant impact on earnings or recorded hours in any occupation. Time savings averaged only a few percent of work hours.

sources.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
sources.publisher: Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen)
sources.text: Using payroll records, we find that since the widespread adoption of generative AI, early-career workers (ages 22-25) in the most AI-exposed occupations have experienced a 13 percent relative decline in employment, even after controlling for firm-level shocks. Employment for more experienced workers in the same occupations has remained stable or grown. Declines concentrate in occupations where AI automates rather than augments work.

sources.title: Mata v. Avianca, Inc.
sources.text: In June 2023 the court sanctioned two lawyers and their firm, imposing a $5,000 penalty, after they submitted a brief citing judicial opinions that did not exist and had been generated by ChatGPT. The judge wrote that there is nothing inherently improper about using a reliable artificial intelligence tool for assistance, but that attorneys remain responsible for the accuracy of their filings.

sources.title: Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models
sources.publisher: arXiv / Journal of Legal Analysis (Dahl, Magesh, Suzgun, Ho)
sources.text: We find that legal hallucinations are alarmingly prevalent, occurring between 69% of the time with ChatGPT 3.5 and 88% with Llama 2, when these models are asked specific, verifiable questions about random federal court cases. Models often fail to correct a user's incorrect legal assumptions and cannot reliably predict when they are producing hallucinations.

sources.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
sources.publisher: Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013 (Dell'Acqua et al.)
sources.text: For tasks within the frontier of AI capabilities, consultants using AI completed 12.2% more tasks on average, completed tasks 25.1% more quickly, and produced results of more than 40% higher quality. For a task selected to be outside the frontier, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions than those without AI.

sources.title: Why Are There Still So Many Jobs? The History and Future of Workplace Automation
sources.text: Automation does indeed substitute for labor, as it is typically intended to do. However, automation also complements labor, raises output in ways that lead to higher demand for labor, and interacts with adjustments in labor supply. Journalists and even expert commentators tend to overstate the extent of machine substitution for human labor and ignore the strong complementarities.

sources.title: Toil and Technology
sources.text: Since ATMs were widely deployed, the number of full-time-equivalent bank tellers has grown. ATMs reduced the number of tellers needed per branch, which made branches cheaper to operate, so banks opened more branches. Tellers shifted toward relationship tasks such as marketing and customer service.

sources.title: ABA issues first ethics guidance on a lawyer's use of AI tools (Formal Opinion 512)
sources.text: Lawyers using generative artificial intelligence tools must fully consider their applicable ethical obligations, including their duties to provide competent legal representation, to protect client information, to communicate with clients, to supervise their employees and agents, to advance only meritorious claims and contentions, and to charge reasonable fees.

sources.title: The Potentially Large Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Economic Growth
sources.publisher: Goldman Sachs Global Economics Analyst (Hatzius et al.)
sources.text: We estimate that roughly two-thirds of current jobs are exposed to some degree of AI automation, and that generative AI could substitute up to one-fourth of current work. Extrapolating globally, generative AI could expose the equivalent of 300mn full-time jobs to automation. We estimate that 44% of tasks in legal professions could be automated. Most exposed jobs are more likely to be complemented rather than substituted.

sources.title: Accountants and Auditors: Occupational Outlook Handbook
sources.text: Employment of accountants and auditors is projected to grow 6 percent from 2023 to 2033, faster than the average for all occupations. About 130,100 openings for accountants and auditors are projected each year, on average, over the decade.
